title: Industrial Inorganic Chemistry: Ammonia, Acids and Alkalis
description: The Haber–Bosch, Ostwald, contact, Solvay and chlor-alkali processes, and hydrogen from steam reforming.
overview: A small group of inorganic chemicals underpins the modern economy: ammonia and nitric acid for fertilizer and explosives, sulfuric acid for fertilizers and metallurgy, sodium carbonate for glass, chlorine and sodium hydroxide for plastics, paper and water treatment. Each is made on a scale of 10⁷–10⁸ tonnes per year, from cheap raw materials (air, water, natural gas, sulfur, salt, limestone), by processes in which equilibrium, kinetics and heat integration were optimized over a century.

The chapter treats each process the way an industrial chemist does: the chemistry, the thermodynamic constraints (Le Chatelier’s principle applied to temperature and pressure), the catalyst, the engineering solution, and the stoichiometric and energetic bookkeeping.
objectives: Apply Le Chatelier’s principle and the van ’t Hoff equation to choose conditions for Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis, and calculate an equilibrium composition.
Describe hydrogen production by steam reforming and the water–gas shift reaction.
Write the reactions of the Ostwald process and the contact process, including double absorption.
Explain the Solvay process and its recycling of ammonia.
Describe the membrane chlor-alkali cell, and calculate its energy consumption from Faraday’s laws.
Do mass-balance calculations for tonnage of raw materials and products.

sections.title: Ammonia: the Haber–Bosch process
body: Ammonia is the key to fixed nitrogen. The **Haber–Bosch process** (Haber 1909, scaled by Bosch at BASF in 1913) combines nitrogen from air and hydrogen:

body.eq: N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g)    ΔH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹ (of reaction as written),   ΔS° = −198 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

body: The reaction is exothermic and reduces the number of gas molecules from 4 to 2. By **Le Chatelier’s principle**, high pressure and low temperature favor ammonia. The equilibrium constant K_p = p²(NH₃)/[p(N₂)p³(H₂)] falls with temperature according to the van ’t Hoff equation: it is about 6 × 10⁵ atm⁻² at 298 K but only 1.45 × 10⁻⁵ atm⁻² at 500 °C. At 298 K the reaction is thermodynamically very favorable but kinetically impossible, since N≡N (945 kJ mol⁻¹) is so strong that the uncatalyzed reaction has a prohibitively high barrier. The practical conditions are a compromise between equilibrium and rate:

head: Variable
Value
Reason
rows: Needed for a useful rate with the catalyst; lower T gives better equilibrium but too slow
Shifts the equilibrium to NH₃; higher pressure costs compression energy and stronger vessels
Fe (from Fe₃O₄), promoted with K₂O, Al₂O₃, CaO
Dissociates N₂ at the surface (the rate-limiting step); K donates electron density, Al₂O₃ stabilizes the surface area
Stoichiometric mixture gives the highest equilibrium yield
Ammonia removed by cooling and condensation (partial pressure ≈ 30–40 atm); unreacted gas recycled
Per-pass conversion only 15–25%; removal of NH₃ shifts the equilibrium; > 97% overall
table.caption: Conditions in the Haber–Bosch process.

example.title: Equilibrium conversion
example.problem: At 500 °C K_p = 1.45 × 10⁻⁵ atm⁻². For a stoichiometric feed at a total pressure of 200 atm, what mole fraction of NH₃ is at equilibrium?
example.solution: For the mixture with mole fractions y(NH₃) = y, y(N₂) = (1−y)/4 and y(H₂) = 3(1−y)/4: K_p P² = y²/[((1−y)/4)(27(1−y)³/64)] = 256y²/[27(1−y)⁴]. With K_pP² = 1.45 × 10⁻⁵ × 4.0 × 10⁴ = 0.58: y²/(1−y)⁴ = 0.58 × 27/256 = 0.0612, so y/(1−y)² = 0.2474. This is 0.2474y² − 1.4948y + 0.2474 = 0, so y = 0.170. At 17 mol% NH₃ at the outlet, the equilibrium has been approached; at 50 atm (K_pP² = 0.036) the conversion would fall to y ≈ 0.05.

body: Hydrogen for ammonia (and for refining and methanol) is made mostly by **steam reforming** of natural gas over a nickel catalyst: CH₄ + H₂O ⇌ CO + 3 H₂ (ΔH° = +206 kJ mol⁻¹), at 800–900 °C and 20–30 atm in tubes heated externally. The reaction is strongly endothermic and increases the number of gas moles, so high temperature and moderate pressure (a compromise with the downstream compression) are used. In a second (secondary) reformer air is added, burning some of the gas to supply heat and also the nitrogen needed. The CO is converted in the **water–gas shift** reaction, CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂ (ΔH° = −41 kJ mol⁻¹; Fe₃O₄/Cr₂O₃ at ≈ 400 °C and Cu/ZnO at ≈ 200 °C), then CO₂ is scrubbed (with amine solutions) and the remaining CO and CO₂, which poison the iron catalyst, are converted to CH₄ by methanation. The overall energy use of modern plants is ≈ 28 GJ per tonne NH₃, close to the thermodynamic minimum of 20 GJ, and ≈ 1.2% of the world’s CO₂ emissions arise from ammonia production (1.9 t CO₂ per t NH₃, and it is the target of “green ammonia” with electrolytic hydrogen).

Most ammonia (80%) goes to fertilizers, directly or as **urea** (2 NH₃ + CO₂ → NH₂COONH₄ → (NH₂)₂CO + H₂O, 46% N), **ammonium nitrate** (NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃, 35% N) and ammonium sulfate and phosphates. The rest produces nitric acid, explosives, nylon and acrylonitrile.

example.title: Mass balance
example.problem: How much hydrogen and nitrogen are needed to produce 1.00 t of ammonia, ideally?
example.solution: 1.00 × 10⁶ g/17.03 = 5.87 × 10⁴ mol NH₃. H₂ = 1.5 × 5.87 × 10⁴ = 8.81 × 10⁴ mol = 178 kg; N₂ = 0.5 × 5.87 × 10⁴ = 2.94 × 10⁴ mol = 823 kg. The hydrogen requires (from CH₄ via 4 H₂ per CH₄ overall) about 0.35 t of methane (CH₄ + 2 H₂O → CO₂ + 4 H₂) for the hydrogen alone.

check.q: Why is the Haber–Bosch process run at 400–500 °C even though low temperature favors NH₃?
check.a: The catalyst needs the temperature for an acceptable rate

check.q: What is the function of potassium in the iron catalyst?
check.a: It acts as an electronic promoter, facilitating N₂ dissociation

check.q: Why is CO removed before the synthesis loop?
check.a: CO and CO₂ poison the iron catalyst

sections.title: Nitric and sulfuric acids
body: Nitric acid is made by oxidizing ammonia (the **Ostwald process**) in three steps:

list: 4 NH₃ + 5 O₂ → 4 NO + 6 H₂O   ΔH = −905 kJ. Ammonia and air (10% NH₃) pass over a **platinum–rhodium gauze** catalyst at 800–900 °C and 1–10 atm, with a contact time of ~10⁻³ s. The yield of NO is 95–98%. The reaction is very exothermic, so it is autothermal. The short contact time matters: with a longer contact, NO decomposes (2 NO → N₂ + O₂) or ammonia reacts with NO to give N₂, which is thermodynamically more stable, so selectivity is under kinetic control.
2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂   (the cooled gas oxidizes without catalyst; the reaction is third-order and exothermic, the rate increases at low temperature, a rare negative temperature coefficient).
3 NO₂ + H₂O → 2 HNO₃ + NO   in the absorption tower; the NO is reoxidized and recycled. The product is 55–68% HNO₃, and concentration to 98% needs dehydrating distillation (azeotrope at 68%).

body: Overall: NH₃ + 2 O₂ → HNO₃ + H₂O. Most nitric acid is neutralized with ammonia to make ammonium nitrate; some goes to adipic acid and explosives (TNT, nitroglycerin). The tail gas is treated by catalytic reduction to remove NO_x (and N₂O, a by-product of the oxidation).

example.title: Nitric acid from ammonia
example.problem: What mass of HNO₃ (100%) can be made from 1.00 t of NH₃ at an overall yield of 94%?
example.solution: 1 mol NH₃ → 1 mol HNO₃: 63.01/17.03 = 3.70 t per t NH₃ in theory; at 94%, 3.48 t HNO₃ (about 5.7 t of 61% acid).

body: Sulfuric acid is the most produced chemical (≈ 2.5 × 10⁸ t y⁻¹; 60% for phosphate fertilizer). Sulfur (from the Claus process of desulfurization of oil and gas, or from the Frasch process) is burned in dry air: S + O₂ → SO₂ (ΔH = −297 kJ mol⁻¹). The heart of the **contact process** is the oxidation:

body.eq: 2 SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2 SO₃    ΔH° = −198 kJ mol⁻¹

body: It is exothermic and reduces the gas moles from 3 to 2, so the equilibrium is better at low T and high P; but the reaction is slow below ≈ 400 °C. The catalyst is **vanadium(V) oxide** (V₂O₅ with K₂SO₄ promoter, molten on silica support), active from ≈ 400 °C. The gas passes through several catalyst beds (the **converter**) at 400–450 °C, with cooling between the stages to maintain a favorable equilibrium; the first bed starts at ≈ 600 °C (fast, 70% conversion), and the final beds are at 400–430 °C. Pressure is kept at ≈ 1–2 atm because the conversion is already 99+% and compression is not needed. The SO₃ is not absorbed in water (the reaction forms an uncontrollable mist) but in 98% H₂SO₄: SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (**oleum**, pyrosulfuric acid), which is diluted with water: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2 H₂SO₄. In **double absorption**, the gas is passed to an absorption tower after the third bed, the SO₃ is removed (shifting the equilibrium), and the remainder is returned to the fourth bed: the total conversion rises from 98% to 99.7%, with emissions of SO₂ reduced.

example.title: Sulfuric acid from sulfur
example.problem: How many tonnes of H₂SO₄ (98.08 g mol⁻¹) result from 1.00 t of sulfur at 99.5% overall conversion? How much heat is released if all steps are exothermic with SO₂ → SO₃ at −99 kJ per mol SO₃ and S → SO₂ at −297 kJ per mol?
example.solution: 1 mol S → 1 mol H₂SO₄: 98.08/32.06 = 3.059 t per t S; at 99.5%, 3.04 t. Heat: per mole of S, −297 − 99 = −396 kJ plus the heat of hydration of SO₃ in water (≈ −130 kJ): about −525 kJ per mol H₂SO₄, or 5.4 GJ per tonne of acid, and the plant recovers it as high-pressure steam (a modern sulfuric acid plant is a net exporter of energy).

check.q: Why is the Ostwald oxidation of NH₃ done with a very short contact time on the Pt–Rh gauze?
check.a: To make NO selectively, before NO decomposes or reacts with NH₃ to form N₂
wrong: To avoid melting the gauze only

check.q: Why is SO₃ absorbed in 98% H₂SO₄ rather than water?
check.a: Water gives a fine acid mist that is hard to collect; the strong acid absorbs SO₃ smoothly as oleum

check.q: What is the purpose of double absorption?
check.a: Removing SO₃ mid-process shifts the equilibrium so the final conversion is higher (≈ 99.7%)
wrong: It lowers temperature in the burner

sections.title: Sodium carbonate, chlorine and sodium hydroxide
body: Sodium carbonate (**soda ash**, Na₂CO₃) is needed for glass (about half), detergents, and chemicals. The direct reaction 2 NaCl + CaCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ is thermodynamically unfavorable, so the **Solvay (ammonia–soda) process** (1863) takes an indirect route using the low solubility of NaHCO₃, with ammonia as a recycled intermediate:

list: NaCl(aq) + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃↓ + NH₄Cl   (CO₂ is bubbled through ammoniated brine in a tower at 30–40 °C; sodium bicarbonate is the least soluble salt present and precipitates)
2 NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O   (calcination of the filtered solid at 160–200 °C; CO₂ is recycled)
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂   (limestone kiln at 900–1000 °C; the CO₂ goes to step 1)
CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂;   2 NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → 2 NH₃ + CaCl₂ + 2 H₂O   (ammonia is recovered and recycled)

body: Overall: 2 NaCl + CaCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂. Ammonia is a catalyst-like intermediate (almost wholly recycled), the raw materials are cheap, and the only by-product is calcium chloride solution (a disposal problem). Where natural trona (Na₂CO₃·NaHCO₃·2H₂O) is mined, as in Wyoming, it is cheaper to refine the mineral (this has displaced Solvay plants in the USA).

example.title: Raw materials for soda ash
example.problem: What masses of NaCl and CaCO₃ are needed to make 1.00 t of Na₂CO₃ (105.99 g mol⁻¹)?

body: The electrolysis of brine gives three products at once: chlorine (PVC, solvents, disinfectants, titanium dioxide), sodium hydroxide (paper, alumina, soap, chemicals) and hydrogen:

Anode: 2 Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (E° = +1.36 V; the overpotential of O₂ evolution is high on the catalytic electrode, so chloride is oxidized in preference to water, E° = +1.23 V). Cathode: 2 H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2 OH⁻ (E° = −0.83 V at pH 14). The thermodynamic minimum cell voltage is ≈ 2.2 V, and in practice 3.0–3.3 V. Three cell types exist. The old **mercury cell** (the Na⁺ is reduced to sodium amalgam at a Hg cathode, then reacts with water to give pure NaOH) has been phased out because of mercury pollution (Minamata). The **diaphragm cell** has an asbestos or polymer diaphragm and gives dilute NaOH contaminated with NaCl. The modern **membrane cell** separates the compartments with a cation-exchange membrane of perfluorinated sulfonate polymer (**Nafion**), which passes Na⁺ (and water) and blocks Cl⁻ and OH⁻, producing a pure 32% NaOH solution; the anode is titanium coated with RuO₂/IrO₂ (a **dimensionally stable anode**), the cathode nickel. The brine must be purified of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ (precipitated as CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂, then ion-exchange), which would foul the membrane.
The products appear in a fixed ratio: per tonne of Cl₂, 1.128 t NaOH (the “electrochemical unit”, ECU) and 28 kg of H₂. The process uses about 2% of the world’s electricity.

example.title: Energy of the chlor-alkali process
example.problem: Compute the electrical energy to make 1.00 t of Cl₂ at a cell voltage of 3.0 V and 95% current efficiency.
example.solution: n(Cl₂) = 1.00 × 10⁶/70.90 = 1.41 × 10⁴ mol; 2 mol e⁻ per mol → 2.82 × 10⁴ mol e⁻ × 96,485 C = 2.72 × 10⁹ C (ideal). With 95% efficiency, charge = 2.86 × 10⁹ C. Energy = QV = 2.86 × 10⁹ × 3.0 = 8.6 × 10⁹ J = 2390 kWh. The industry figure is 2200–2600 kWh per tonne Cl₂. Over half the cost of chlorine is electricity.

check.q: Why can NaHCO₃ be precipitated from the Solvay mixture?
check.a: It is the least soluble salt present in the cold ammoniated brine

check.q: What does the Nafion membrane do in a chlor-alkali cell?
check.a: Passes Na⁺ but blocks Cl⁻ and OH⁻, so the NaOH is pure

check.q: What mass of NaOH is produced per tonne of Cl₂?

quiz.q: In Haber–Bosch synthesis at fixed temperature, the total pressure is doubled. What happens?
quiz.a: K_p is unchanged, but the equilibrium mole fraction of NH₃ rises
wrong: K_p doubles, and the NH₃ mole fraction doubles with it
K_p is unchanged, and the NH₃ mole fraction is also unchanged by pressure
K_p rises with pressure, but the NH₃ mole fraction stays the same
quiz.why: An equilibrium constant depends only on temperature. Pressure shifts the composition: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol, so more pressure favors NH₃.

quiz.q: The conversion per pass through the ammonia reactor is only 15–25%, yet more than 97% of the feed ends up as NH₃. How?
quiz.a: NH₃ is condensed out and the unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled
wrong: The catalyst is regenerated after each pass
The pressure is raised on each successive pass, which raises K_p
Unreacted gas is burned to supply heat for the reactor
quiz.why: Cooling removes NH₃ as a liquid, which also pulls the equilibrium toward product, and the leftover reactant gases go back to the reactor. Pressure changes the composition but not K_p.

quiz.q: Why is steam reforming (CH₄ + H₂O ⇌ CO + 3 H₂, ΔH° = +206 kJ mol⁻¹) run at 800–900 °C but only 20–30 atm?
quiz.a: Heat favors the endothermic reaction, but high pressure favors fewer gas moles and would work against it
wrong: The reaction is exothermic, so heat favors the products, and moderate pressure saves compression energy
The nickel catalyst melts or sinters if the pressure rises above about 30 atm
High pressure favors the products because the reaction makes more gas, so only heat is limiting
quiz.why: Reforming absorbs heat and raises the moles of gas from 2 to 4. Le Chatelier's principle makes high temperature useful and high pressure counterproductive, apart from the downstream compression cost.

quiz.q: How many moles of H₂ can be obtained from 1.00 mol of CH₄ by steam reforming followed by complete water–gas shift?
quiz.why: Reforming gives CO + 3 H₂, and the shift CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂ adds one more H₂ per CO, so 4 mol in all. Stopping after reforming would give 3.

quiz.q: What mass of N₂ is required to make 3.00 t of NH₃?
quiz.why: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, so 28.01 g of N₂ gives 2 × 17.03 g of NH₃. The mass is 3.00 × 28.01/34.06 = 2.47 t. The 0.53 t figure is the H₂ requirement.

quiz.q: At 298 K, K_p for N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃ is about 6 × 10⁵ atm⁻², yet N₂ and H₂ do not react without a catalyst. Why?
quiz.a: K_p says nothing about rate; the strong N≡N bond gives a high barrier
wrong: The large K_p means that the equilibrium lies on the side of N₂ and H₂, so no NH₃ forms
The reaction is endothermic at low temperature, so it only goes when heated
K_p exceeds 1 only above 400 °C, so nothing forms before that point
quiz.why: The thermodynamics are very favorable at 298 K. The problem is kinetic, which is why a catalyst and 400–500 °C are used.

quiz.q: How many tonnes of HNO₃ result from 2.00 t of NH₃ at an overall yield of 90%? (Use NH₃ → HNO₃, 17.03 and 63.01 g mol⁻¹.)
quiz.why: One mole of NH₃ gives one mole of HNO₃, so the ideal ratio is 63.01/17.03 = 3.70 and the mass is 2.00 × 3.70 × 0.90 = 6.66 t. Omitting the yield gives 7.40.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the oxidation 2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂ in the Ostwald process?
quiz.a: It speeds up as the temperature falls
wrong: It needs the Pt–Rh gauze at 900 °C to proceed
It is endothermic but still spontaneous
It is strictly first order in NO and O₂ together
quiz.why: The reaction is exothermic and third order, with a negative temperature coefficient of the rate, so the gas is cooled before oxidation.

quiz.q: In the absorption tower, 9.0 mol of NO₂ react with water by 3 NO₂ + H₂O → 2 HNO₃ + NO. How many moles of HNO₃ form in this step?
quiz.why: Three moles of NO₂ give two of HNO₃, so 9.0 mol give 6.0 mol. The NO produced is reoxidized and recycled.

quiz.q: In a contact-process converter the first bed is near 600 °C and the later beds at 400–430 °C. Why?
quiz.a: A hot first bed is fast while far from equilibrium; cooler later beds give high conversion
wrong: The catalyst is only active near 600 °C and must be cooled to avoid melting in later beds
The reaction is endothermic, so heat is needed at the start and less is needed later on
Lower temperatures in the later beds give a faster rate, which the final conversion needs
quiz.why: The oxidation of SO₂ is exothermic, so equilibrium improves as the gas is cooled, while a high temperature gives the fast rate at the start.

quiz.q: Single absorption gives 98% conversion of SO₂, and double absorption gives 99.7%. How does the unconverted fraction change?
quiz.why: The unconverted amounts are 100 − 98 = 2% and 100 − 99.7 = 0.3%. Removing SO₃ in the middle lets the remaining gas react further.

quiz.q: How many tonnes of sulfur are needed to make 10.0 t of 98.0% H₂SO₄ (98.08 g mol⁻¹), assuming complete conversion?
quiz.why: The acid contains 9.80 t of H₂SO₄ = 0.100 × 10⁶ mol, and each mole needs 1 mol of S: 0.100 × 10⁶ × 32.06 g = 3.20 t. The value 3.27 t ignores the 98% strength.

quiz.q: How is ammonia recovered and recycled in the Solvay process?
quiz.a: NH₄Cl is treated with Ca(OH)₂ made from the limestone kiln product CaO
wrong: NH₄Cl is electrolyzed in a membrane cell to give NH₃ and Cl₂
NH₄Cl is reduced with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst
NH₃ is released when the NaHCO₃ solid is calcined in the kiln
quiz.why: 2 NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → 2 NH₃ + CaCl₂ + 2 H₂O. Calcination of NaHCO₃ releases only CO₂ and water, and CaCl₂ is the process's only by-product.

quiz.q: What mass of NaCl is required to make 5.00 t of Na₂CO₃ (105.99 g mol⁻¹)?
quiz.why: Overall 2 NaCl + CaCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂, so 5.00 × 2 × 58.44/105.99 = 5.51 t. The value 2.76 t forgets the factor of 2.

quiz.q: Why must the brine fed to a membrane cell be purified of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺?
quiz.a: They precipitate as hydroxides in the membrane and foul it
wrong: They are reduced at the cathode and so waste a part of the current
They corrode the titanium anode coating over time
They react with the Cl₂ that is released to form chlorates
quiz.why: The cathode compartment becomes strongly alkaline, so Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ that cross or enter the membrane form solid hydroxides. That raises resistance and ruins the membrane.

quiz.q: Using E° = +1.36 V for Cl₂/Cl⁻ and −0.83 V for water reduction at pH 14, what is the thermodynamic minimum voltage of the chlor-alkali cell?
quiz.why: The cell voltage is E(anode) − E(cathode) = 1.36 − (−0.83) = 2.19 V. Subtracting the magnitudes gives 0.53 V. Real cells operate at 3.0–3.3 V because of overpotentials and resistance.

quiz.q: How much electricity is needed to make 1.00 t of Cl₂ at 3.0 V and 90% current efficiency?
quiz.why: 1.00 t Cl₂ is 1.41 × 10⁴ mol, which needs 2.82 × 10⁴ mol e⁻ = 2.72 × 10⁹ C ideally. Dividing by 0.90 gives 3.02 × 10⁹ C, and × 3.0 V = 9.07 × 10⁹ J = 2520 kWh. Multiplying by 0.90 would wrongly lower it.

quiz.q: A plant makes 50.0 t of NaOH per day in a membrane cell. How much Cl₂ does it make in the same time?
quiz.why: 2 NaCl + 2 H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2 NaOH, so 70.90 g of Cl₂ comes with 2 × 40.00 g of NaOH: 50.0 × 70.90/80.00 = 44.3 t. Multiplying by 1.128 inverts the ratio.

summary: Haber–Bosch: N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ). Equilibrium favors low T, high P; the Fe catalyst needs 400–500 °C, so 150–300 atm and a recycle loop with NH₃ condensation are used (≈ 17% at equilibrium, 200 atm, 500 °C). H₂ comes from steam reforming (CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3 H₂, +206 kJ) and the water–gas shift.

Ostwald: 4 NH₃ + 5 O₂ → 4 NO + 6 H₂O on Pt–Rh gauze (800–900 °C, short contact time), then NO → NO₂ → HNO₃ by absorption. Contact: S → SO₂ → SO₃ over V₂O₅ at 400–450 °C in multi-bed converters with double absorption; SO₃ is absorbed in 98% H₂SO₄ to make oleum.
Solvay: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl, calcination, ammonia recycled with lime. Net: 2 NaCl + CaCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂.
Chlor-alkali: electrolysis of brine in a membrane cell gives Cl₂, H₂ and NaOH (1.13 t NaOH per t Cl₂), at ≈ 3 V and ≈ 2400 kWh per tonne of Cl₂.

problems.q: Use ΔH° = −92.4 kJ and ΔS° = −198 J K⁻¹ (per 2 NH₃) to estimate K_p at 298 K and 773 K, assuming constant ΔH° and ΔS°. Compare the result at 773 K with the experimental value of 1.45 × 10⁻⁵ atm⁻².
problems.solution: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. At 298 K: −92.4 + 298 × 0.198 = −33.4 kJ → K = exp(33,400/(8.314 × 298)) = exp(13.5) = 7 × 10⁵. At 773 K: −92.4 + 773 × 0.198 = +60.6 kJ → K = exp(−60,600/(8.314 × 773)) = exp(−9.43) = 8 × 10⁻⁵. The estimate (constant ΔH, ΔS) is a few times larger than the real value because ΔH becomes less negative with the temperature; but it shows the sign of the effect: K falls by a factor of 10⁹ from 298 to 773 K.
problems.a: K(298) ≈ 7 × 10⁵; K(773) ≈ 10⁻⁴: the equilibrium falls with the temperature by about nine orders of magnitude.

problems.q: A converter feed has 11% SO₂, 10% O₂, 79% N₂ (by volume). If 98% of the SO₂ is converted, find the composition of the exit gas on 100 mol of feed.
problems.solution: SO₂ in = 11 mol; converted = 10.78 mol → SO₂ = 0.22 mol; SO₃ = 10.78 mol. O₂ consumed = 5.39 → O₂ = 4.61 mol. N₂ = 79 mol. Total = 0.22 + 10.78 + 4.61 + 79 = 94.61 mol. Mole fractions: SO₃ 11.4%, SO₂ 0.23%, O₂ 4.9%, N₂ 83.5%.

problems.q: A Solvay plant has an overall yield of 92% on NaCl. How much brine (25% NaCl by mass) is needed to make 100 t of soda ash per day?
problems.solution: 100 t Na₂CO₃ = 9.435 × 10⁵ mol requires 2 × 9.435 × 10⁵ = 1.887 × 10⁶ mol NaCl = 110.3 t NaCl in theory. At 92%: 119.9 t NaCl. At 25% NaCl: 479.6 t of brine (≈ 480 t) per day.

problems.q: Why can chloride be oxidized at the anode in preference to water in brine electrolysis, although the standard potential for oxygen evolution is lower?
problems.solution: Oxygen evolution from water is kinetically slow (a four-electron process with a high overpotential, 0.5–1 V on typical electrodes), while Cl⁻ oxidation is a fast two-electron process. On RuO₂-based anodes the overpotential for O₂ is large and that for Cl₂ is small (< 0.05 V), so at practical current densities chloride is oxidized selectively (with a current efficiency of 95–97%). The high concentration of Cl⁻ in saturated brine (≈ 5 M) also favors the reaction. In acid solution, E for O₂ is less favorable by the pH effect as well.
